title: Not yours to finish (Avot 2:16)
hookLine: Rabbi Tarfon: it is not yours to finish the work, nor are you free to give it up
last: START WITH THE THING THAT MATTERS MOST.

cards: Some problems are too big for one life. Hunger. Loneliness.
A broken family pattern that goes back generations. A neighborhood that needs a hundred things. You look at them and two feelings arrive together.
One says, it's hopeless, why bother. The other says, it's all on me, and I'm failing. Both are exhausting, and both make people quit.
In the very next line, Rabbi Tarfon answers both at once, in a sentence people have been writing on walls and in notebooks ever since.

teach.b: It is not upon you to finish the work.
But you are not free to walk away from it. Two halves, and each answers a different fear. To the one who says it's all on me: it isn't.
You were never asked to finish. The work is bigger than one life, and it was always meant to be. You do your part, and hand it on.
To the one who says it's hopeless: you're still not free to quit.
The Hebrew phrase is ben chorin, a free person, the same words used for a slave who's been set free. You're not that kind of free, not from this. You still owe your piece.
The Talmud has a story that fits right beside it.
Honi, a well-known sage, is walking along a road when he sees an old man planting a carob tree. How long until it gives fruit? Honi asks.
Seventy years, says the man. Do you really think you'll live seventy more years? And the old man answers: I found carob trees in the world when I came into it.
My ancestors planted them for me, and I'm planting for my children.
He won't finish. He won't eat the fruit. And he plants anyway.
Rabbi Tarfon ends by returning to the employer from two days ago: the one you work for is trustworthy, and will pay your wage. You don't have to see the harvest to know the planting counts.

how: Rabbi Tarfon's words are among the most quoted in Pirkei Avot, often cited by Jews working on long efforts for justice, learning and repair that no one person can complete.

o: a free person, like a slave who's been set free
a student who has finished all of his learning
a son of the priests who served in the Temple

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.
p: a free person, like a freed slave

s: Rabbi Tarfon says you must finish what you start
he says it is not upon you to finish the work.
Rabbi Tarfon says you're free to quit if it's hopeless
you are not free to walk away from it.
in the Talmud, the old man plants a carob tree he may never eat from
my ancestors planted for me, he says, and I plant for my children.

games.q: you're an old man by the road with a carob seedling. it won't bear fruit for seventy years. what do you do?
o: don't bother. you'll never eat from it.
plant it for the ones who come after you.
games.why: he planted it: my ancestors planted for me, and I plant for my children.

practice: Think of one big problem that weighs on you, in your family, your town, the world, and let yourself feel how big it is. Then set down the part that was never yours, finishing it, and feel that weight go.
Now find your piece, the small, real part you could do, one call, one hour, one kindness, one seed, and hold it in your hands.

wordCard.voice: Ben chorin. A free person: what Rabbi Tarfon says you're not, not free to walk away from work that isn't yours alone to finish.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: it is not upon you to finish the work.

carryVoice: Your line: don't finish, don't quit. The old man planted anyway. Day two hundred sixty-four is planted.
